description: We do not accept more people
summary: No place on Earth is Mars or the Moon. The useful question is how far a place goes, and where the analogy breaks down. Sealometro is an open similarity-ranking tool that answers it with NASA and partner data. Our engine compares 41 Earth locations (22 new candidates, mostly in Bolivia and Latin America, plus known analogs and negative controls) with 12 targets, including Jezero, Gale, Gusev and Meridiani on Mars, and Artemis III regions, the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge and lava-tube pits on the Moon. For each pair it reports the similarity per dimension, the progress from a typical Earth place toward the target, and Earth's limits (pressure, gravity, radiation) as gaps. Key result: Bolivia's Siloli desert scores 61/100 against Gale crater, within one point of Atacama–Yungay, a classic analog. We do not hide weaknesses: missing data is never filled in, scores are withheld below 40% data coverage (still the case for the lunar south pole), and our weak validation (AUC 0.56) is published as is. A low-cost ESP32 field box measures the place, a web station checks each sensor against independent references, and a phone turns the site into a map where you drive a rover under Mars or Moon gravity.
details:
Live app (no login): https://seal-box.web.app/?lang=en · Open code: https://github.com/CamiloNunezArroyo/sealometro

What it does. Sealometro answers three questions about a place on Earth: How similar is it to one specific site on Mars or the Moon? How far does it go from a typical Earth place toward that site? Where does the analogy break down?

How it works.

  • Similarity engine (Python). Each place and each target is described by dimensions: mean temperature, day–night range, rain, soil moisture, wind, vegetation (NDVI), albedo, slope and roughness, mineral classes. Per dimension a Gaussian kernel gives a similarity; the Index of Analogy is a weighted mean over the dimensions that have data.
  • Progress instead of a zero. Even on the high Altiplano Earth's air is far too thick (at Siloli, 88 times Jezero's pressure), so a plain distance gives every place a zero. We measure the share of the way from the median Earth place to the target: Sucre covers about 6% of the way to Jezero's pressure, and Siloli's soil is drier than 92% of our Earth reference sample.
  • Gaps stay gaps. Gravity, atmosphere and pressure are shown as numbers Earth cannot reach and are never scored. Radiation dose is shown as "pending" because we have not yet verified a source.
  • Field box. An ESP32 with BME280, GUVA-S12SD UV, light, MQ gas and MPU-6050 sensors and an LCD sends a reading every 0.5 s over Wi-Fi (median upload 0.4 s, measured). The station page grades each sensor against independent references (Open-Meteo weather, Copernicus DEM) and computes the analogy of the measured place with the same math as the engine, checked by tests against the Python engine.
  • Playable place. Phone photos and a 10-second video (indoors), or GPS, OpenStreetMap and relief (outdoors), build a map of the real place where you drive a rover with Mars or Moon gravity. The image analysis is simple and explainable; no AI model is involved.

What we found.

  • Against Gale Crater, the known analog Atacama–Yungay ranks first (61.2/100), and the Bolivian candidate Siloli desert is within one point of it (60.6/100), staying in the top 3 in 98% of 2,000 Monte Carlo runs that vary our weights and the data uncertainty. Namib–Sossusvlei follows (60/100). These scores use 56% of the weighted dimensions.
  • Against Jezero, Siloli is second (46/100) behind Atacama–Yungay (57/100).

Where it breaks down (our own limits).

  • Validation: known analogs versus 300 random land points give AUC 0.56 for global Mars (90% interval 0.45–0.68, 13 known analogs). For Gale and Jezero alone, it is not better than chance (0.44 and 0.46). The engine recognizes extreme-climate analogs but not yet geological ones, because the random points have no mineral data.
  • Six of the 12 targets (the three Artemis III regions, Shackleton–de Gerlache, global Moon and the Arcadia ice region) get no score yet: coverage is below our 40% minimum or the target values are only estimates. The engine says so and shows the gaps only.
  • Climate comes from a coarse grid (about 50 km). Weights and tolerances are our design decisions, labelled as such.
  • The sensors are low-cost, so each one is graded against a reference before its reading is used.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve. Point mission teams and field scientists to lesser-known, cheaper analog candidates beyond the famous ones, starting with the Bolivian Altiplano; teach what makes Mars and the Moon different, not only what looks similar (three reading levels: ages 8–12, 13–17 and 18+, in English and Spanish); and let any school check satellite data with its own instrument. Next steps: mineral and terrain data for the random sample, and LRO Diviner and LOLA data to score the lunar south pole.

Why it is creative. One "Mars-like" score hides the science. We separate similarity, progress and gaps, keep missing data visible, and close the loop from satellite data to a field measurement to a place you can play in.

Tools. Python 3.11 (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, rasterio, pydantic, typer, pytest, h5py); TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Three.js (104 automated tests in the web app); ESP32 with Arduino core 3.x, ArduinoJson, Adafruit BME280; Firebase Realtime Database and Hosting; Web Serial.

Prior work and AI. The rover game started as a prototype the team made a few days before the hackathon. The engine, field box, station page, and integration were built during it. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for code, source checking and drafting; files carry an AI-assistance header and the log is in docs/AI_USE.md. No AI-generated images, audio or video. No NASA logos.
